idiom_name: discriminated union + exhaustive switch (never-checked default) dispatcher
implementation_notes: TypeScript keeps the routing decision at the type level: define each message as a member of a discriminated union (a literal kind field), switch on it so every branch narrows the payload type - a handler cannot receive the wrong shape - and make the default arm assign to never, which turns an unhandled kind into a compile error; that exhaustiveness check is what replaces a router class and its condition list. Framework routers route on transport metadata rather than content: NestJS @MessagePattern matches the pattern value carried in the message envelope (verified), so a decision that depends on the body still needs this dispatcher, while broker bindings (AMQP headers exchanges, Kafka topics and headers) route on keys chosen at publish time. Validate the discriminant with a schema library at the boundary so the compiler's guarantees start from checked data.
pitfalls: The messages arrive as unknown JSON: a type assertion to Msg is a lie until a schema validator (zod, io-ts, ajv) checks the discriminant, so an invalid message reaches a handler with the wrong branch's assumptions.
The exhaustiveness guarantee disappears the moment the default arm does something other than assertNever (or is dropped in favour of logging), and nothing else re-checks the union.
Transport-level patterns (@MessagePattern) match the envelope pattern, not the payload body, so routing that needs body content must not be delegated to the transport.
